summary:
İstanbul stands under the national framework in force across Turkey. Kaos GL's 2025 annual report, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", records state-policy hostility toward LGBTI+ people operating in the city directly, including intensified practices of sealing or closing the homes of LGBTI+ residents that obstruct access to housing. The same monitoring counts six violations of the right to life across Turkey in 2025, three recorded as hate-motivated, with trans people the group most affected; torture and ill-treatment violations nearly doubled to 89 from 51; one LGBTI+ association was closed with criminal cases opened against 11 members; and the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics.

Street-level policing in İstanbul targets trans women specifically. On 31 July 2025 police in Beyoğlu stopped around 20 trans women for ID checks while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station, recorded their names and took videos of them; bianet's report characterises the operation as profiling.

The Governorship of İstanbul has denied permission for and locally banned pride parades in the city since 2015 on security and public-order grounds, with the 2016 to 2018 bans stated explicitly and water cannon used on 29 June 2015. Police suppression escalated in the years that followed: blockades and tear gas in 2021 with 25 people arrested; 373 arrested in 2022 as public transport to Taksim Square was shut down; 113 arrests in 2023; and 11 arrests in 2024, three of them minors, after organisers moved İstanbul Pride to non-Taksim public spaces and issued fake meeting calls to thwart police. The 2014 march drew over 100,000 participants, the largest LGBT event in Turkey's history.

On 26 June 2022 riot police dispersed the Pride march at Taksim Square, blockaded streets in the nearby Cihangir neighbourhood, shut down public transport to the square and detained 373 people, including AFP photojournalist Bülent Kılıç, who were released after a night in custody according to Kaos GL. The district governor's offices of Kadıköy and Beyoğlu had banned all Pride Week events for seven days.
tangentialFactors:
Duvar English reported on 27 June 2022 that Turkish authorities have banned Pride since 2014 and that police crackdowns on the parades have grown harsher over the years, a trajectory the İstanbul arrest figures track from 25 in 2021 to 373 in 2022.

Organisers' adaptation in 2024, relocating events away from Taksim Square and issuing decoy meeting points, indicates that police monitoring of Pride communications is expected and that participation carries an identification risk even where no arrest follows.
localsOnly:
Residents of İstanbul face housing obstruction through intensified sealing or closing of LGBTI+ homes recorded in Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring, and the closure of one LGBTI+ association with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members.

The Governorship's standing ban on pride parades since 2015 constrains resident organising: Kadıköy and Beyoğlu district governor's offices have issued seven-day bans covering all Pride Week events, and arrests have included minors.

The state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so residents cannot rely on official data to document or contest anti-LGBTI+ violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the national draft legislative package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

The inventory does not document İstanbul-specific incidents of the six right-to-life violations or the 89 torture and ill-treatment cases counted nationally in 2025, so their distribution within the city is not sourced.
